$comment: Buildings (v0.1, Roluos era). size = footprint in tiles (1 tile = 2 m). buildSec = seconds for one villager (more builders are faster). hp, armor for combat. pop = population room it adds. dropOff = resources villagers may leave here. trains / researches = what its command panel offers. cost is paid when the foundation is placed; cancelling refunds refundShare of it (rules.json).

buildings.notes: Royal and elite dwellings were wooden and have not survived; as a gathering and training point it is a gameplay abstraction.

Pteas Rong (PK 1.8.0, after his 889 CE brief: late Chenla, early Angkor): and his reference picture): two steep thatch gables side by side with bamboo battens over the thatch and horn finials at the apexes, woven bamboo walls with awning windows, a railed veranda reached by a wooden stair, a split-bamboo floor raised about 1.9 m on square hardwood stilts standing on carved stone pedestals (not buried in the earth), facing east; the open undercroft shows the farm's daily life: firewood, baskets, an ox cart, clay water jars, straw, a fish trap. No spirit house: that custom is recorded much later. PK's reference says the Rong type goes back to the Funan period, the oldest of the five types; no Angkor-period wooden house survives, so the form is a reconstruction from the later tradition.

Pteas Keung: the tallest type, the house of officials and dignitaries: a steep high gable over a lower hipped roof all round, a front porch under its own gable and a grand stair (PK's reference). Wooden houses of the 12th century do not survive; the type is known from the later tradition, so its Angkorian form is uncertain.
A place to bring goods close to work. Granaries and stores surely existed, but no Roluos-period store has been identified.

A log yard near the forest: woodcutters stack timber here and ox-carts take it to the storehouse (PK). Ox-carts with solid wheels hauling goods appear on the Bayon reliefs; the yard itself is a gameplay abstraction.
Bunded rice fields around Hariharalaya are visible in the archaeological landscape.
Khmer armies were levied; a permanent barracks is a gameplay abstraction for where troops gather and train.
The temple of the current chapter (campaign.json): Preah Ko, Bakong, Lolei… Costs and build times are gameplay abstractions; real temples took years.

A wooden landing on posts at the water's edge, with a store shed (PK: build a port for the big ships). Zhou Daguan (1296) describes the Chinese merchants coming by sea and up the river to the lake; boats are carved on the Bayon. The junk orders come only when a landing stands. The layout is a game abstraction.

Zhou Daguan (1296-97): the market is held every day from early morning to noon; the trading is done by women, who lay mats on the ground with no shops, each paying the officials for her place. Here: mats, baskets of goods and light thatched shades on an open ground. In Anachak Khmer, goods are exchanged here at rates that move with trade.
